The remainder of the taught stroke regimen infuses over 60 minutes.
Recognize important bleeding during antithrombotic treatment.
Exclude intracranial hemorrhage and verify eligibility before stroke thrombolysis.
Acute neurological worsening during thrombolysis needs immediate escalation.
Stroke thrombolysis timing follows current eligibility guidance and local protocol.
Apply the taught 0.9 mg/kg stroke dose with 90 mg maximum.
Distinguish pre-treatment BP eligibility from post-thrombolysis limits.
Follow post-thrombolysis monitoring/imaging before antithrombotic treatment.
ACS includes unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI.
Unstable angina is ischemia without biomarker evidence of necrosis.
NSTEMI does not require persistent ST elevation.
Recognize an ischemic symptom cluster.
Initial ACS assessment includes vitals, monitoring, prompt ECG, access, and escalation.
Reduced coronary blood flow produces acute myocardial ischemia.
Use oxygen when oxygenation or clinical status indicates it.
Do not delay escalation of concerning ischemia while awaiting biomarkers.
An acute ischemic presentation with ST elevation needs urgent assessment.
Third-degree AV block produces independent atrial and ventricular activity.
Identify AV dissociation on ECG.
A slow escape rhythm can reduce output and organ perfusion.
Review reversible contributors including rate-slowing medicines and electrolyte problems.
Sinus bradycardia preserves conducted P/QRS relationships.
Escalate symptomatic CHB and prepare for pacing.
Correlate a conduction pattern with the patient’s perfusion.
Hypoxia and hyperkalemia are reversible contributors to conduction deterioration.
A diagnostic 12-lead ECG uses ten physical electrodes.
An electrode is a physical contact; a lead is an electrical view.
V1 electrode position.
V2 electrode position.
V3 electrode position.
V4 electrode position.
V5 electrode position.
V6 electrode position.
P wave electrical meaning.
QRS complex electrical meaning.
T wave electrical meaning.
IEC RA/R color.
IEC LA/L color.
IEC LL/F color.
IEC RL/N color.
In IEC limb labels F means Foot and N means Neutral.
High V1/V2 placement can produce a misleading tracing.
V5 and V6 share V4’s horizontal level.
Ten electrodes can generate twelve derived views.
Telemetry monitoring and diagnostic 12-lead ECG have different roles.
ECG and pleth arise from different physiological signals.
Interpret rate and intervals with the patient and P/QRS relationship.
Estimate rate from a six-second strip.
Recognize the taught normal PR and QRS intervals.
A common basic telemetry setup uses three electrodes.
Use the 300 method only for a regular rhythm.
Assess the patient and pulse when a tracing may be artifact.
A pleth pulse signal does not replace a diagnostic ECG.
VF and pulseless VT are shockable arrest rhythms.
PEA and asystole are non-shockable arrest rhythms.
PEA is electrical activity without a palpable pulse.
Pulse status separates pulseless VT from pulse-present VT management.
Hypotension, altered consciousness, shock, ischemia, or acute HF indicates instability.
An organized ECG does not exclude cardiac arrest.
Defibrillation is unsynchronized treatment for VF/pVT arrest.
Synchronized cardioversion treats selected unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse.
Synchronization avoids the vulnerable repolarization period.
Pacing supports dangerous symptomatic bradycardia/high-grade block.
Electrical capture is a pacing spike followed by a QRS complex.
Polymorphic VT may require unsynchronized shock.
Confirm electrical and mechanical capture.
Choose electrical treatment from pulse status, rate, and stability.
Assess the patient and ABCs before relying on the monitor label.
Use focused ABCDE assessment to identify immediate problems.
Recognize sudden clinical red flags.
Reassess after interventions.
Exposure assessment includes bleeding, lines, edema, and visible causes.
Treat a pulseless unresponsive patient as an arrest.
Prepare support while escalating an evolving respiratory/perfusion problem.
A dangerous monitor pattern needs immediate patient and pulse correlation.
Cardiogenic shock is pump failure with organ hypoperfusion.
Recognize a low-perfusion cluster.
MI, severe HF, arrhythmia, and mechanical problems can impair the pump.
Recognize distributive and obstructive shock mechanisms.
A large automatic fluid bolus may worsen pulmonary edema in pump failure.
Differentiate pump failure from volume-loss patterns using the full picture.
A BP value must be interpreted with organ perfusion.
Norepinephrine primarily supports vascular tone and pressure.
Dobutamine primarily supports contractility and output.
Monitor rhythm, pressure, urine output, and peripheral perfusion.
Pressure and pump support may be combined.
mL/hour depends on the ordered dose and prepared concentration.
Convert a specified infusion dose and concentration into mL/hour.
Norepinephrine monitoring includes peripheral IV site ischemia/extravasation signs.
Low potassium can cause flat T waves/U waves and arrhythmia.
Low magnesium can contribute to ventricular arrhythmia and refractory hypokalemia.
Calcium affects QT in opposite directions when low or high.
Never give IV potassium as a rapid IV push.
Severe high potassium can widen QRS and produce bradyarrhythmia/arrest.
Loop-diuretic-associated PVCs warrant potassium and magnesium review.
Magnesium is important in torsades de pointes.
Furosemide treats congestion and fluid overload.
Furosemide is a loop diuretic that increases urine output.
Monitor BP, fluid status, kidney function, and potassium.
Evaluate breathing and edema, not urine volume alone.
New ectopy during diuresis can be electrolyte-related.
Excess diuresis can cause volume depletion, hypotension, and renal deterioration.
Heart failure can involve congestion, inadequate output, or high filling pressures.
Identify pulmonary/systemic congestion.
Identify poor perfusion in HF.
Left and right ventricular failure produce different backup patterns.
EF describes the fraction of LV blood ejected, not the whole clinical severity.
Preserved EF does not exclude clinically important HF.
Congestion and poor perfusion can coexist.
Acute respiratory or perfusion deterioration in HF needs escalation.
DCM has ventricular dilation and weak systolic contraction.
DCM can present with HF and arrhythmia.
Myocarditis, inherited disease, or cardiotoxic exposures can contribute to a DCM phenotype.
Recognize familial, inflammatory, toxic, peripartum, and tachyarrhythmic contributors.
Track the clinical weak-pump consequences.
Monitor rhythm and perfusion as well as congestion.
IHD is a broad coronary blood-supply disease state.
MI involves myocardial necrosis from ischemia.
Not every IHD presentation is an MI.
The relationship is broad disease versus a specific necrotic event.
Assess distal blood supply and nerve function below an injury/immobilization.
Pain, circulation, sensation, movement, and swelling form the focused check.
Raised compartment pressure can reduce perfusion and damage nerve/muscle.
Disproportionate pain, especially with passive stretch, is an early warning.
Immobilization modification and invasive treatment need authorization.
Pallor, paralysis, and absent pulses are late ischemic findings.
A palpable pulse does not rule out compartment syndrome.
Escalate deterioration within supervised intern scope.
Do not normalize a new severe pain trend as ordinary fracture pain.

External fixation can suit severe open/soft-tissue-compromised fractures.
Use the limb–pins–frame–patient bedside structure.
New pin-site redness/drainage/fever can indicate infection.
Pin care follows aseptic technique and the authorized local plan.
Use aseptic pin care with the authorized product and schedule.
Assess the limb before focusing on hardware.
Loose or broken hardware needs protection and escalation, not independent adjustment.
Assess the whole patient and wound, report deterioration, document, and reassess.

The principal hexapod arrangement has six adjustable struts.
Pins/wires connect bone to the external rings.
TSF may be used for complex fractures, deformity, lengthening, or reconstruction.
Correction follows a surgeon-planned individualized schedule.
Distal neurovascular assessment precedes frame-focused reassurance.
Recognize pin infection, hardware failure, skin pressure, and alignment red flags.
Document time, change, baseline comparison, notification, instructions, and response.
Trained patient self-adjustment does not authorize an intern to improvise.
Pulses can persist during early compartment syndrome.
Weight bearing and wound/pin care follow prescribed orders.
Reassess after a clinical change or intervention.
Assess and document skin pressure points near the frame.
Osteomyelitis is bone infection with possible blood, contiguous, or direct entry.
Recognize persistent deep pain, drainage, poor healing, and inflammation.
Assess vitals, wound/drainage, pain trend, and neurovascular status.
Treatment may include prolonged antibiotics and surgery/debridement.
Bone infection may arise through bloodstream, contiguous spread, or direct inoculation.
Chronic drainage is not automatically normal.
Escalate systemic deterioration or worsening infection/hardware problems.

sourceUnitPolicies.reason: Provenance, stock observations, catalogue metadata, and evidence notes are not independent nursing knowledge objectives. Clinical instructions in administration/monitor/use/mechanism remain in scope.

sourceUnitPolicies.lessonSections: memory/summary sections repeating an already taught clinical point
sourceUnitPolicies.reason: Repeated wording does not need a duplicate question. Keep the underlying clinical point in the bank.

sourceIssues.detail: The source lists ischemic heart disease/previous MI as a DCM cause. The ESC cardiomyopathy definition distinguishes a DCM phenotype from dysfunction explained solely by coronary disease or abnormal loading.
sourceIssues.handling: Do not key a question that teaches coronary disease alone as sufficient for the strict DCM diagnosis. Other listed contributors remain testable. Source wording needs separate review.

coverageReview.reason: The generated point-to-question map records what is actually tested. It does not certify that the complete source has been reduced to an exhaustive required-point inventory.
coverageReview.rule: An untested clinical fact cannot be reclassified as background merely to make coverage appear complete.

questionDesignExclusions.detail: A separate class-recall question is omitted because the full class label is already supplied by the displayed medication name. Its principal action and clinical information remain tested separately.
